docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I am Justice Chukwuemeka, a Junior Systems Engineer in the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information Technology Job Rotation Program.

I am on my third rotation, at the Center for High Throughput Computing (CHTC). There I work on Linux infrastructure, HTCondor operations, storage systems, and the research computing environments that scientists rely on to run large jobs.

Before CHTC, I worked on the DoIT General Help Desk, where I learned troubleshooting and support from the user side, and then on the DoIT Public Cloud Team, where I worked on AWS, governance, and automation. That path, from supporting users to running cloud services to running research infrastructure, is why I care about systems that are reliable, well documented, and easy to operate.

What I am working toward now is straightforward: become a strong systems engineer, built from the foundations up. That means Linux first, then networking, then systems operations, with depth in networking. For my fourth rotation, I am looking for infrastructure or networking work.

This portfolio is a record of that work. The case studies show how I approached real problems, what I tried, and what I learned, not just a list of tools I have touched.

docs.title: Career Growth
docs.text:
I want to become a highly technical systems engineer, and I want to get there without skipping steps.

Right now that means learning Linux properly. I spent my first few months reading documentation constantly just to get things done, and I am working through that stage on purpose: practice every day, build labs, and do not run a script I cannot explain line by line. Networking comes next, then systems operations, then depth in networking.

That plan also guides what I am looking for next. For rotation 4, I want infrastructure or networking work, not another generalist stop. After the program, I am tracking systems roles in Wisconsin, where I can keep doing this kind of work at scale.

The through line is simple. I started by helping individual users, then I helped run cloud services, and now I help run research infrastructure. I want the next step to go deeper in the same direction.

docs.title: HTCondor Node Troubleshooting
docs.text: Linux HTCondor Distributed Computing Troubleshooting

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: I investigated an HTCondor execution node in the CHTC environment, e2466.chtc.wisc.edu, that did not appear to be functioning as expected. The node was visible in HTCondor status information, which indicated that it was successfully advertising itself to the collector. The node was not accepting jobs.

docs.title: The central question
docs.text:
The investigation turned on a distinction that mattered for the whole diagnosis: a node being visible to the collector is not the same as a node actually being available to run jobs. If I had stopped at visibility, the node would have looked healthy. The question I had to answer was why a node that was advertising itself was not behaving like a healthy execution node.

That question was sharper because of the node's recent history. The node had been drained and rebuilt about two days earlier, so it should have been receiving jobs again by the time I investigated it.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
I connected to the node with SSH and ran condor_status. That confirmed the starting observation: the node was present in HTCondor status information, yet it was not accepting jobs.

From there, I checked the temporary Condor configuration file, htcss.testing.config, where temporary Condor configurations are written. In that file, I found a line setting PreventJobsReason, a setting that gives a reason why a job should be prevented from running on a specific node. That line explained the symptom I was seeing. The node could advertise itself to the collector while still being prevented from accepting jobs.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text: I commented out the PreventJobsReason line and restarted Condor. I then checked the Condor systemd service with systemctl status condor to confirm that the service was running. I also checked the process tree and confirmed that condor_master, condor_shared_port, and condor_startd were present.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: After the fix, I verified the node by watching its behavior rather than relying on visibility alone. Queued jobs claimed different slots on e2466, which showed that the node was accepting work as an execution point should.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: I restored the node to service as an execution point that could accept queued jobs. I do not have a number for the scale of the impact, and I am not estimating one here. In a system that queues jobs, an execution point that cannot accept jobs reduces the capacity available to that queue, so restoring a node that should already have been back in service mattered even without a job count attached to it.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This case demonstrates structured troubleshooting of a distributed system, end to end. I started from a precise symptom, separated visibility from availability, checked temporary configuration before assuming a deeper failure, made a single targeted change, and verified the result by watching jobs claim slots on the node.

docs.title: Migrating 930 GiB Past a CephFS Quota Failure
docs.text: Linux rsync CephFS Storage Troubleshooting

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: I received a request to move a dataset of over 930 GiB from /home/h/<user_redacted>/DSCOVR to /staging/h/<user_redacted>. I chose rsync over a plain mv because rsync can resume after a failure instead of starting over. That choice paid off: the transfer failed partway through, and the fix required understanding CephFS directory quotas.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Shortly after I initiated the move, rsync failed with:

Disk quota exceeded (122)
rsync error: error in file IO (code 11)
rsync: [sender] write error: Broken pipe (32)

The destination filesystem had free space, so the quota being exceeded was not the disk filling up. It was a CephFS directory quota on the destination path, a separate administrative limit from overall capacity. Acting on the face-value reading, finding more space, would have wasted the effort; the actual limit was a quota that someone had to raise.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text: I investigated the CephFS quota wrapper scripts, set_cephfs_dir_quota_items and set_cephfs_dir_quota_size, to understand how the cluster applied quotas to directories. The scripts ultimately expanded into setfattr commands setting ceph.quota.max_bytes and ceph.quota.max_files on the directory. That told me exactly which two settings controlled the failure. They were the maximum file count and the maximum byte count under the destination path.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
I asked one of the research computing facilitators (RCFs) what the quotas should be, and they specified 500,000 files and 1.5 TiB. I set the file count quota first:

set_cephfs_dir_quota_items 500000 /staging/h/<user_redacted>

Then the size quota, passing gibibytes as the script expects (1.5 TiB is 1536 GiB):

set_cephfs_dir_quota_size 1536 /staging/h/<user_redacted>

The script converted 1536 GiB to bytes (1536 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024) and applied it via setfattr. With both quotas raised, I re-ran the rsync migration. Because rsync resumes rather than restarts, the transfer picked up where it had failed instead of re-sending 930 GiB from scratch. I monitored it through to verified completion.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: The full dataset migrated successfully once the CephFS quotas reflected the actual need. The value of the work was in two decisions: choosing rsync up front so a failure would be resumable, and reading the quota wrapper scripts to learn the mechanism instead of guessing.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This case demonstrates storage troubleshooting that goes below the surface, combined with deliberate tool choice. When rsync reports a quota error but the filesystem has free space, the right move is to identify the actual quota mechanism, in this case CephFS directory quotas applied through setfattr, and work with it directly. The failed first attempt cost minutes instead of hours because rsync resumes where it stopped, while mv would have started over.

docs.title: Recovering a Chromebook from Cryptohome Failure
docs.text: ChromeOS Crostini Endpoint Support Troubleshooting

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A student's Chromebook could not launch its Linux terminal, and the repair path led through a ChromeOS update into a cryptohome mount failure that locked the student out of the device entirely. A Powerwash reset resolved it. The case is a clean example of escalation discipline: non-destructive steps first, documented procedures next, destructive reset only after I had exhausted the alternatives.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: The student needed terminal access, so I started the penguin container, the default Crostini Linux container on ChromeOS. It failed with Error starting crostini for terminal: 62 (NEED_UPDATE). The error code pointed at the operating system itself: the installed ChromeOS version was too old for the terminal to start. That made the next step obvious, but the step after it was not.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text: Following a documented troubleshooting path, I updated ChromeOS on the device, which is the reasonable response to a NEED_UPDATE error. The update completed and I rebooted. The student then could not sign back in at all: the device reported can't mount crypto home. Cryptohome is ChromeOS's encrypted per-user storage, so a mount failure there means the user's entire profile, including the Crostini container, is unreachable. I worked through the troubleshooting steps in Google's support documentation for this exact error, and none of them resolved it.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text: With the documented non-destructive steps exhausted, I reset the Chromebook with a Powerwash, which returns it to its factory state. That resolved the mount failure and the device came back healthy. A Powerwash erases local data, so this was not a step to take lightly; it was the last resort after the update path and the support documentation both failed. I want to report the outcome precisely: I restored the device to service, but I do not have a record of which local files, if any, the student lost in the reset.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: The student got a working device back the same day instead of a multi-day repair cycle. The case stayed at the help desk the whole way through: terminal error, OS update, sign-in failure, documented troubleshooting, and finally the reset. Each step followed from the evidence of the previous one rather than from guessing.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This case demanded disciplined endpoint troubleshooting under a real constraint. The NEED_UPDATE error had one reasonable response, and that response created a worse problem, which is exactly when discipline matters most: I worked the documented steps, confirmed each failure before moving on, and took the destructive step only after nothing else remained. It also demonstrates working knowledge of the ChromeOS stack, including Crostini containers, cryptohome, and the recovery procedures around them.

docs.title: Diagnosing an MFA Browser Compatibility Issue
docs.text: MFA FIDO2 Authentication Customer Support

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A user on macOS could not complete Passwordless authentication in Firefox. The credentials were valid and the user had hardware-based authentication available, but the login would not finish. The cause was a documented browser limitation, not anything wrong with the user's account or devices, and the fix was guidance, not a configuration change.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: The failure was specific to the browser. The user had Touch ID and a security key available on macOS, and both should have worked for Passwordless login. In Firefox, neither did. That pattern pointed away from the account or the authenticator and toward how Firefox handled the authentication flow on macOS.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text: I traced the login attempt to the exact point of failure: the step where the browser hands off to the hardware authenticator. Per Duo's documentation, Firefox on macOS does not support Touch ID because it lacks the necessary FIDO2 support, and it cannot prompt for the security key's PIN to satisfy the Passwordless user-verification requirement. On macOS, Firefox only supports Duo Push for Passwordless authentication. That confirmed the issue was browser-dependent. The user's credentials, security key, and enrollment were all fine; the browser simply could not complete the ceremony the login required.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: With the cause confirmed in Duo's documentation, I explained the limitation in plain terms and guided the user to authenticate with Duo Push, the supported Passwordless method in Firefox on macOS. The user had walked in thinking their key or account was broken, and the fix needed them to understand that neither was true. No account changes, no re-enrollment, no weakening of the security posture.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: I unblocked the user in a single support interaction, with no backend intervention. The case never needed to leave the tier where it arrived; it needed someone to identify that the browser, not the identity, was the problem, and to translate that finding into an action the user could take immediately.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This case came down to separating the layers of an authentication failure. Credentials, authenticator, and browser were three different suspects, and the evidence pointed at the browser. It also shows the value of checking vendor documentation before acting: without the Duo article confirming the Firefox on macOS limitation, the easy move would have been churning the user's account settings while the real cause sat untouched in the browser.

docs.title: Resolving a Python Environment Issue for Coursework
docs.text: Python Conda Troubleshooting Customer Support

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A student could not complete coursework because the required Python version would not run on their laptop. The course needed Python 3.10.12, but the student's Anaconda installation had set up Python 3.13. Two commands in the terminal fixed it, plus one more for the dependency error that surfaced underneath.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: The student had installed Python through Anaconda, which pulled the recent 3.13 release. Their coursework specifically required 3.10.12, and the newer version would not run what the course needed. The machine was fine and the installation was healthy; it was simply the wrong version. The fix had to swap the Python version inside the existing Anaconda setup without disturbing anything else on the system.

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text: The reported symptom was "Python 3.10.12 does not work," which could have meant many things. Checking the actual environment showed the real situation: there was no 3.10.12 on the machine at all, only the 3.13 that Anaconda had installed. That reframed the problem from something broken to something missing. The fix was a version change, not a repair, which meant the risk was low as long as the change stayed inside the Conda environment.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text: From the terminal I ran conda install python=3.10.12, which downgraded the environment's Python to the required version. That surfaced the next layer: importing packages failed with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named menuinst. Following a documented resolution for this exact error, I ran conda install menuinst, which resolved the missing module. After both installs, the environment executed the coursework successfully.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: I unblocked the student, who continued coursework the same day. I resolved the issue at the help desk without escalation, which would have cost the student days of waiting for a problem that turned out to need two package installs. The value of the work was in the diagnosis: verifying what was actually installed before acting, rather than treating "does not work" as a single problem with a single fix.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This case rewarded structured troubleshooting and restraint. I checked the ground truth first and fixed the specific mismatch instead of escalating, which would have cost the student days of waiting. Version changes in Conda frequently surface dependency errors like the missing menuinst module, and resolving them in sequence instead of starting over is what keeps a ten-minute fix from becoming a reinstall.

docs.title: Service Account Governance for a Student Organization
docs.text: IAM Identity and Access Management Security Customer Support

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A registered student organization needed shared communication channels and a website presence that would survive changes in its leadership. The request arrived at the help desk as a routine access question, but the correct answer depended on governance, not just tooling.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: The organization needed shared access to communication and online resources. The expedient option would have been a personal NetID belonging to a current officer, but that would have tied ownership of the organization's accounts to one individual. Student organizations turn over their leadership every year or two, so the failure mode was not hypothetical. When the account holder graduated or stepped down, the organization would have faced lockouts, awkward credential handoffs outside any approved process, and an audit trail that pointed at a person who was no longer involved. The request needed a solution designed for shared, long-term ownership rather than individual convenience.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text: I evaluated the request against identity management best practices and the university's account governance policies instead of treating it as a simple provisioning ticket. The review came down to a lifecycle question: who owns this access in two years, and how does it transfer? A personal NetID had no good answer. That pointed to service accounts as the appropriate mechanism, since service accounts exist for shared organizational use rather than being tied to one person's identity, and their ownership can move with the organization's leadership. I escalated the request to the Productivity and Collaboration Services (PCS) team, which owns service account provisioning, rather than trying to implement it from the help desk.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: To be clear about the boundary of my involvement: PCS contacted the customer directly and took the request from there, so I did not see the final provisioning through and cannot confirm that PCS created the accounts. I identified the correct mechanism, verified it against policy, and routed the organization to the team that owns it, which avoided the continuity and security risks a personal NetID would have created as leadership turned over. Because I routed it correctly at the start, nobody had to unwind a personal-account setup later.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: Support work is not only about fixing what is broken. It also means recognizing when the expedient handling of a request would create a larger problem later. This case shows governance-aware triage. I worked from the identity model behind the request, reasoned about the full lifecycle of the access being granted, chose the mechanism that fit the organization's actual lifespan, and routed the work to the right owners instead of improvising a shortcut that the next officer would inherit as a crisis.

docs.title: Mapping AI Service Support Ownership
docs.text: Cloud AI SaaS Technical Research Stakeholder Collaboration

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: As providers expanded their AI offerings, the university needed to decide which AI services it would officially support, and which team would own that support: PCS (Productivity and Collaboration Services, essentially the SaaS team) or the Public Cloud team. I contributed license research on eight Google AI services, linked into a spreadsheet table, as the first step in that decision.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: New AI services were arriving faster than support decisions. Without knowing each service's licensing terms, the university could not determine which services it could support, under what terms, or which team should own them. The decision involved important stakeholders because it would set which AI tools the university stood behind.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
I researched license information for eight Google AI services: NotebookLM, Gemini Workspace (Web Assistant), Workspace Studio, Antigravity CLI, Jules, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Gemini Looker, and Vertex AI. I linked each service's license information into a spreadsheet table so the decision-makers could compare them side by side. That table was the first step toward answering the ownership question: for each service, PCS or Public Cloud.

To be honest about my role: my contribution was the license research and the table. The support-ownership decision itself was made by others. But I was in the conversations where the university worked through which AI services it would support, and that is the part of this work I value most.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: The spreadsheet gave stakeholders a single reference for license terms across the eight services, feeding directly into the PCS-versus-Public-Cloud support decision. I do not know whether the guide saw continued use after the decision, and I am not claiming more than the research step I owned.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This case shows I am comfortable operating one level up from the keyboard. I turned a vague institutional question, which team supports which AI service, into a concrete research artifact with license terms linked and comparable, so that decision-makers could actually use it. It also shows I understand the support boundary problem from both sides, having worked on the Public Cloud team while coordinating with PCS, the SaaS team.

docs.title: AWS Innovation Sandbox
docs.text: AWS Terraform AWS Control Tower GitLab

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The DoIT Public Cloud Team needed a sandbox where researchers could experiment with AWS services without risking production accounts or breaking institutional guardrails. The project started as a direct ask from a Research facilitator consultant and was not on the team's roadmap for the year. I joined it during my rotation and worked with Kelly Rivera, the Cloud Engineer Lead.

docs.title: The central question
docs.text: AWS ships the Innovation Sandbox as a set of CloudFormation deployment templates. The Public Cloud Team runs a 100 percent Terraform environment. The question was how to take templates designed for CloudFormation and deploy the whole sandbox through Terraform without losing what the templates were built to do.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text: I sat in the requirements meetings where we worked out what the sandbox had to do, alongside the consultant and the team. Then I wrote the Terraform in live coding sessions over Teams video calls, with Kelly directing each session and telling me what to do as we went. I wrote the Terraform that deployed the AccountPool stacks, the IDC stack, the Data stack, and the Compute stack. Because the AWS templates were written for CloudFormation, I modified the .template and .yaml files so Terraform could deploy them.

docs.title: Blocker 1: no API for third-party SAML apps
docs.text: The sandbox needs single sign-on, and AWS does not expose API endpoints to fully automate provisioning a third-party SAML application through the Terraform AWS provider. The provider's ssoadmin_application resource documents what is possible, and full automation of that step is not among it. That meant the SAML application step could not be folded into the Terraform deployment like everything else. It had to be handled outside the automated path.

docs.title: Blocker 2: template size limit
docs.text: The InnovationSandbox-Compute.template file exceeded the maximum template size that Terraform accepts for a deployment. The file was simply too large to deploy directly. To get past it, I created a centralized S3 bucket with Terraform to store the ISB CloudFormation templates, and the deployment referenced the templates from the bucket instead of pushing the full file contents through Terraform.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: I rotated off the team before the project finished, so I did not see the final deployment myself. After my rotation I checked in with the Public Cloud team, and they told me the project is now complete and fully deployed. The groundwork I contributed, the Terraform stacks and the S3 workaround, was part of what got it there.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This project shows I can take vendor templates built for one tool and make them work in another. I wrote Terraform for real multi-stack deployments under direction, and I diagnosed exactly where a provider's automation stops. The SAML gap was not a bug in our code. It was a missing API, and naming that precisely is what kept the team from burning time trying to automate the unautomatable.

docs.title: Cloud Security Assessment Framework
docs.text: Risk Management Security Frameworks CIS NIST 800-53

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: During my rotation with the DoIT Public Cloud Team, I helped build a standardized set of security assessment questions for evaluating risk in cloud-based projects. The team had no consistent way to assess a project's security posture early, so gaps surfaced late or not at all. Nine questions, each mapped to CIS and NIST 800-53 controls, now give the team's engineers a repeatable starting point for cloud security reviews.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Cloud projects on the team varied widely in architecture, data handling, and access design, and there was no standard assessment to catch security gaps before projects moved forward. The team needed a short, practical question set that engineers could use with project stakeholders to surface risk early in the project lifecycle.

docs.title: How we worked
docs.text: This was a collaboration with Pam Snyder, the team's cloud security analyst. We held project meetings at least twice a week. Pam led on the security concepts, since that is her specialty, and each meeting established what needed to be done next. Because she was busier than I was, I wrote each question, and in the following meeting we reviewed them together and cross-matched every question to the relevant NIST and CIS controls. The questions cover four areas: data storage and protection, identity and access management, resource governance, and network access.

docs.title: The questions
docs.text:
Three examples show the shape of the set:

  • "Have you assigned a specific individual or role to regularly review and remediate security findings from the cloud provider security tools (e.g., AWS Security Hub, Microsoft Defender for Cloud)?"
  • "Do you enforce least privilege access by granting only the specific permissions required and restricting to only the necessary IP ranges, services, or resources?"
  • "Have you applied the Shared Security Responsibility Model (SSRM) for your project, clearly identifying which security controls are your responsibility and which are inherited from the Cloud Service Provider (CSP)?"

Each question is written so a project owner can answer it directly, and each maps to specific controls so engineers can trace an answer back to the framework behind it.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: Before my rotation ended, I had drafted all nine questions, we had matched them to CIS and NIST controls, and we sent the set to the team's Cloud Engineers for review. The review was still open when I rotated off. I met with Pam afterward and she confirmed the engineers finished their reviews. The plan is to use the question set for cybersecurity assessments of cloud-based projects to evaluate security risk. I do not have a count of projects assessed with it, since that work happened after I left, so I will state the outcome plainly: a completed, peer-reviewed framework ready for use.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: I can take a security concept from a senior analyst and turn it into a concrete, usable work product. I drafted precise questions, mapped them to framework controls, and drove the review to completion across the team. We collaborated throughout: Pam set the security direction while I produced the drafts and the control mappings we reviewed together.

docs.title: Jira Cloud Automation Rules
docs.text: Jira Cloud Automation Regex

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: During my rotation with the DoIT Public Cloud Team, I built seven Jira Cloud automation rules that triaged cloud alert tickets and kept stale tickets moving. One rule processed roughly 500 AWS health alert tickets. It populated their fields and then closed them. Others moved untouched tickets into an autoresolution flow. Regex did the heavy lifting of pulling cloud account IDs out of ticket text, since Azure, AWS, and GCP each use a different ID format.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: There were two problems. First, an alert queue automation created before my time collected every AWS health alert ticket into one queue. Over time the ticket count kept growing, clogging the UI and burying anything important. That is classic alert fatigue: when everything is an alert, nothing is. Second, tickets that went stale sat untouched with no nudge to the owner, so the backlog grew instead of resolving.

docs.title: How I built it
docs.text: I used Jira Cloud's built-in automation engine, no plugins. The core technique was regex. The rules needed the cloud account ID from each ticket's body or description to populate fields, but the three providers format IDs differently: Azure uses a GUID for the subscription ID, AWS uses a 12-digit numeric account ID, and GCP uses a project ID of 6 to 30 characters. One regex per format let a single rule handle tickets from all three clouds.

docs.title: The automations
docs.text:
Three examples from the seven rules:

  1. AWS health alert triage. The rule picked up the backlog of about 500 AWS health alert tickets, populated fields including project, cloud provider, and cloud account ID (extracted with regex), then transitioned each ticket to Done. The rule retained critical alerts instead of sweeping them up in the bulk close.
  2. Stale ticket nudge. Tickets with no modification for one week moved to "Pending - Autoresolution," and the rule emailed the ticket owner and requestor asking for action.
  3. Auto-close. The rule closed tickets automatically after another week in "Pending - Autoresolution".

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: The alert queue went from roughly 500 open alert tickets to a clean queue with only critical alerts retained, which cut the noise the team had to wade through every day. Stale tickets now get a warning email after a week of inactivity and close after two, instead of lingering indefinitely. I am stating the queue size honestly: about 500 tickets processed by the triage rule, per the backlog I saw.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: This work started from an operational pain point, alert fatigue and ticket rot, and ended with automation handling both. The regex work shows I think about real-world data formats rather than assuming clean input, and the autoresolution flow respects the humans in the loop by warning first and acting second.

docs.title: Auditing 160 Knowledge Base Documents for Accessibility
docs.text: Accessibility Technical Writing Quality Assurance Knowledge Management

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Over about two months, alongside my other rotation work and meetings, I audited roughly 160 articles in DoIT's internal knowledge base platform and remediated the accessibility issues I found, so the documentation worked for everyone, including people using assistive technologies.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: The knowledge base had grown through many contributors with varying accessibility awareness, and the inconsistency was a real barrier, not a cosmetic issue. The recurring problems were concrete: inconsistent heading levels, tables without proper header cells, links whose text did not describe where they led, language that was harder than it needed to be, and code samples wrapped in <pre> tags instead of proper code formatting. Each issue was small; across 160 articles they added up.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text: I worked through the articles systematically with a repeatable pass: read for structure, check formatting consistency, verify accessibility, fix what was broken, and move on. Across the collection I corrected the recurring issue types above and standardized formatting where it had drifted, so the knowledge base reads as one coherent resource instead of 160 individual efforts. When the audit was complete, I presented the work to the team in a standup, walking through what I had found and fixed, and documented a reference framework so authors could write new documents accessibly from the beginning instead of repairing them afterward.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text: About 160 articles reviewed and remediated over roughly two months, interleaved with my other project work and meetings. The knowledge base came out more consistent and more usable, and the reference framework turned a one-time cleanup into a durable standard: each new document starts from an accessible baseline instead of reintroducing the old inconsistencies.

docs.title: What this shows
docs.text: I treated accessibility as engineering work in this case, not a checkbox exercise. I found the recurring patterns, fixed them at scale across 160 articles, and then changed the process so the problems would stop being created. It also shows sustained execution: two months of steady audit work carried alongside everything else on my plate.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Center for High Throughput Computing provides advanced computing resources and expertise to support research and scientific discovery.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
The bulk of my work in this rotation is provisioning and decommissioning hosts. That work includes upgrading nodes to AlmaLinux 10, including nodes in Kubernetes clusters. I also support Linux-based research computing infrastructure, including HTCondor operations and troubleshooting, Ceph storage and data management workflows, and configuration and change management processes using Puppet and Python.

I also do hardware work when troubleshooting requires it. That includes hardware troubleshooting for GPU dropouts and investigating Ceph storage dropouts, alongside routine infrastructure maintenance and system administration in large-scale computing environments.

docs.title: Representative case studies
docs.text:
• HTCondor Node Troubleshooting
  • Data Migration
  • RACADM Maintenance

These cases cover HTCondor execution node behavior and scheduling availability, storage issues affecting research data migration workflows, and server management and maintenance using Dell iDRAC and RACADM tooling. Together with the provisioning and decommissioning work above, they show the core of the rotation, which is host lifecycle work, Linux systems administration, research computing infrastructure, storage systems, enterprise hardware management, and operational troubleshooting in an environment that researchers depend on.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The DoIT General Help Desk is the front line of information technology support for students, faculty, staff, and affiliates at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: I provided Tier 1 and Tier 2 technical support across account management, authentication, endpoint support, and software and hardware troubleshooting. My work included service account requests under identity and access management principles, Duo multi-factor authentication, and FIDO2 authentication. I supported endpoint devices running Windows, macOS, and ChromeOS. I escalated complex cases to specialized support teams, and I documented troubleshooting findings and resolutions for each case.

docs.title: Representative case studies
docs.text:
• Service Account Governance
  • Python Environment Resolution
  • ChromeOS Cryptohome Failure
  • MFA Browser Compatibility

These cases cover service account governance, Python environment and dependency resolution for academic coursework, ChromeOS cryptohome corruption and Linux environment failure, and Duo and FIDO2 browser compatibility. Together, they show the core of the rotation, which was structured troubleshooting, identity and access management, endpoint support, and clear communication with users.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The DoIT Public Cloud Team enables the use of public cloud technologies across the university through consulting, governance, security guidance, and cloud engineering support.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: I worked on cloud architecture, Infrastructure as Code, workflow automation, cloud security, governance, and technical documentation. My work included cloud project discovery and planning, Infrastructure as Code workflows using Terraform, cloud security research, process automation, and improvements to internal documentation and knowledge management resources.

docs.title: Representative case studies
docs.text:
• AWS Innovation Sandbox
  • Jira Automation
  • Cloud Security Assessment Framework
  • AWS AI Security Research
  • Knowledge Base Accessibility Audit

These cases cover the AWS Innovation Sandbox project supporting cloud-based research initiatives, Jira automations that streamlined team workflows, cloud security research covering CIS benchmarks, NIST 800-53, and the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix, internal guidance on AI services and cloud security governance, and an audit of approximately 160 knowledge base documents with remediation of accessibility issues. Together, they show the core of the rotation, which was a move from individual user support to platform-level and organization-level technology solutions.
